slides.label: The showing.
slides.notes: Open cold. Read the finish line out loud and leave it on screen while you set expectations: today ends in a breakout room, and nobody leaves without a dated next step.
slides.html:
Zillow Preferred Onboarding • Day 3

The showing.

Day 2 got the door open. Today you get out of the way — and you do not walk off the driveway with nothing.

Today's finish line

You run a full sidewalk chat in a breakout room, and you come out of it with a real next step.

On a calendar. Not "I'll follow up."

slides.label: Before anything else — a question for the room.
slides.notes: Do not answer it yourself. Wait through the silence — someone always says 'following them around'. Take three or four answers, write them where the room can see, and tell them you will come back to the list.
slides.html:
Before anything else — a question for the room.

You are standing in a house with a buyer you met an hour ago. Answer this honestly.

Stop and talk

What is the fastest way to make a buyer uncomfortable inside a house?

Say it out loud. We will come back to your answers in a minute.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 02 / 31

slides.label: Before you go.
slides.notes: Short divider. Everything in this part happens before the buyer arrives — paperwork out, houses picked, bag packed.
slides.html:
Part one

Before you go.

Paperwork signed, houses picked, bag packed. None of it happens on the hood of your car.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 03 / 31

slides.label: The touring agreement goes out before you go.
slides.notes: Flag the market variation on real-time touring leads honestly — some agents will see these constantly, some almost never. Row three is the one they need: unsigned is normal, handle it at the door.
slides.html:
Paperwork

The touring agreement goes out before you go.

It covers seven days. It is signed ahead of the appointment, not on the hood of your car.

1 Real-time touring lead Sent automatically. How often you see these depends entirely on your market — some are full of them, some almost never.
2 Every other lead You send it yourself, from your Zillow.com Premier Agent profile. The buyer signs by email. It takes a minute.
3 It did not get signed Bring it with you and handle it in person before you open a door. This happens, and it is not a crisis.
This is not the buyer agreement

The touring agreement carries you through the looking. The full one is a different conversation for a different day.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 04 / 31

slides.label: Show two or three. Never one.
slides.notes: Tie this forward: the rating question in part three is worthless with one house. Then sell the buyer packet — most of their buyers have never done this before.
slides.html:
How many homes

Show two or three. Never one.

One house gives a buyer nothing to measure against — and everything you do at the end depends on comparison.

Two or three homes.

In an hour you are going to ask them to rate a house out of ten. That question does almost nothing if there is only one house to rate. Comparison is what makes a buyer tell you what they actually want.

Also in your bag

Comparables for what you are showing.

A buyer packet that walks them through the whole process.

Why the packet matters

Most of your buyers have never done this before. They do not know the steps, how long any of it takes, or what you actually do for them. Something they can read at their kitchen table that night is the cheapest trust you will ever buy — and it answers what they were too embarrassed to ask you.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 05 / 31

slides.label: Inside the house.
slides.notes: Divider. From here to the sidewalk, everything is about what you do with your own body and your own mouth inside somebody else's house.
slides.html:
Part two

Inside the house.

Where you stand, what you say, and everything you are about to stop doing.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 06 / 31

slides.label: You opened the door. Now get out of the way.
slides.notes: Callback to the stop-and-talk. Their answers are almost certainly these three. Land the last line hard: all three feel like good service from the inside, which is why nobody catches themselves doing it.
slides.html:
The pressure

You opened the door. Now get out of the way.

Day 2 said the buyer is deciding who makes this easy. That does not stop when you hand them the key.

Almost every bit of pressure at a showing is unintentional. Nobody sets out to crowd a buyer. They do it by trailing them room to room, by narrating, and by pointing out things the buyer never asked about.

1 Following You walk the house behind them. They cannot react to a room with you watching.
2 Narrating You fill the silence. Every comment is one more thing they have to respond to.
3 Projecting You point out what you like. It is your taste, and they did not ask for it.

All three feel like good service from the inside.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 07 / 31

slides.label: Available, not attached.
slides.notes: This is the physical instruction of the day: let them walk in first, hold the kitchen or the entry, do not follow them upstairs. Read the right-hand list slowly — those four sounds are how they know it is working.
slides.html:
Where you stand

Available, not attached.

The buyer should be able to forget you are there, and find you in four seconds when they want you.

What this looks like

You let them walk in first. You stay near the kitchen or the entry. You do not follow them upstairs. When they call out a question, you are already on your way.

They cannot do this with you behind them
React honestly to a room
Say something unflattering out loud
Talk to each other
Picture themselves living there
This is what you want to hear
Them talking to each other
A door opening twice
Somebody going back to a room
Silence, then a question
TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 08 / 31

slides.label: The trap is your own taste.
slides.notes: Read both parts out loud, agent voice then buyer voice. It gets a laugh, then it lands. The buyer now has to disagree with you inside their own showing.
slides.html:
The trap

The trap is your own taste.

This is a real exchange, and it goes exactly this badly more often than you would think.

Agent

Wow — look at these vaulted ceilings.

Buyer

Well, actually — my wife is incredibly short. The taller the ceilings, the smaller she feels.

What just happened

You gave a preference and called it expertise.

Now they have to disagree with you in their own showing.

You are not there to tell them what is good. You are there to find out what they think is good.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 09 / 31

slides.label: Say the real thing. Skip the rest.
slides.notes: The boundary slide. Left column is your taste in a hard hat. Right column is the stuff they would be angry to learn later. If it changes price or safety, say it.
slides.html:
The line

Say the real thing. Skip the rest.

There is a line between telling a buyer something they need and unloading your opinions on their afternoon.

Nitpicking — leave it alone
A chip in the wall
Paint you would not have chosen
The ceiling fans
A kitchen layout you dislike
Anything the photos already showed
Worth saying out loud
Structural problems
Water where water should not be
Anything that changes the price
Anything that changes safety
Something they would be angry to learn later

Nitpicking feels like being thorough. It lands as pressure — and it is almost always your taste wearing a hard hat.

slides.label: The sidewalk.
slides.notes: Divider. Tell them plainly: this is the part of the day nobody gets trained on, and it is where the money is.
slides.html:
Part three

The sidewalk.

Five minutes, five questions, and the part of the day nobody trained you on.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 11 / 31

slides.label: One more before we go outside.
slides.notes: Make them actually say it, in their own words, before the next slide. Two or three volunteers. Do not correct anything yet.
slides.html:
One more before we go outside.

You have walked three houses. You are standing on the sidewalk and the buyer is reaching for their keys.

Stop and talk

What do you actually say in the next five minutes?

Say it the way you would really say it. We are going to compare it to something in a moment.

Whatever you just said is the part of the day nobody trained you on.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 12 / 31

slides.label: Here is what most agents say.
slides.notes: Read the script flatly and quickly, exactly as it sounds in real life. Then pause before 'Then they leave.' Ask how many of them heard their own answer in it.
slides.html:
The pattern

Here is what most agents say.

Read it and see how much of your own answer is in there.

The agent, wrapping up

It was really nice to meet you. Just wanted to ask — any questions? No? Great. Well, I'm going to follow up, I'll put you on an MLS search, let me know if you see anything. Really excited to help you out on your journey.

Then they leave.

Nothing was established. Nothing was scheduled. You do not know their timeline, you do not know whether they can buy, and you do not know what they actually liked — because you never asked.

You showed up, you showed houses, and you let them walk.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 13 / 31

slides.label: Instead: five questions, in order.
slides.notes: No acronym on purpose. Tell them the order matters more than the wording, and that every question is hypothetical — that is what makes it askable an hour after meeting somebody.
slides.html:
The spine of the closeout

Instead: five questions, in order.

There is no acronym. The questions are the thing to remember, and they run about five minutes on a sidewalk.

1 Did you see one? Did you see any home you want to write an offer on?
2 Rate it. On a scale of one to ten, how would you rate what we saw?
3 Make it an eight. What would have to change for that to be the one?
4 Cash or a lender? If we were writing tomorrow — cash under the bed, or a lender?
5 Why that date? Is your timeline a guess, or does something have to change by then?

Every one of them is hypothetical. You never ask a buyer directly what they can afford or how serious they are.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 14 / 31

slides.label: One — did you see one you'd write on?
slides.notes: The first half of the sentence is the whole trick. Have the room say it back to you once before moving on.
slides.html:
Question one

One — did you see one you'd write on?

You are expecting a no. That is the entire point of asking.

You

I'm sure if you had seen something today that was just the one, you would have told me. But I was curious — did you see any homes you want to write an offer on?

Them

No — not really.

Why it is worded that way

The first half gives them permission to say no.

No pressure, no disappointment to manage. And a no is what opens every question that follows.

If they say yes — congratulations, you have a very different afternoon. Everything below still applies, just faster.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 15 / 31

slides.label: Two — rate it, one to ten.
slides.notes: Contrast the two phrasings out loud: 'how did you like them' gets 'they were fine'. A number gets you a house to aim question three at.
slides.html:
Question two

Two — rate it, one to ten.

A number is easy to give and almost impossible to give vaguely.

You

Well, like I said, I figured you would have told me. I'm curious though — on a scale of one to ten, how would you rate the homes?

Them

The first one, maybe a five. The last one was a seven.

What you just got

A ranking, without asking anybody to explain themselves.

And a specific house to aim the next question at.

"How did you like them?" gets you "they were fine." A number gets you somewhere.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 16 / 31

slides.label: Three — what would make it an eight?
slides.notes: 'Take a trip with me' is the phrase to memorize. Nobody defends a hypothetical — and because they said it, they will not argue with it later.
slides.html:
Question three

Three — what would make it an eight?

This is where the real criteria arrive, and they arrive in the buyer's own words.

You

A five — so not high on our list. That's fair. Take a trip with me. Let's pretend for a moment this home was an eight for you. What would need to change to make you say, hey, this is the home for me?

Them

A real garage. And the kitchen being closed off from the living room drives me crazy.

Take a trip with me

Nobody defends a hypothetical.

Asked directly what they want, buyers recite a wish list. Asked to fix one specific house, they tell you the truth.

You now know what to search on tomorrow — and they said it, so they will not argue with it later.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 17 / 31

slides.label: Four — cash under the bed, or a lender?
slides.notes: Point out what they did not ask. Then tell them to say congratulations to a first-time buyer and mean it — almost nobody does.
slides.html:
Question four

Four — cash under the bed, or a lender?

Still hypothetical. That is the only reason you can ask it an hour after meeting somebody.

You

Let's say it had all of those things — eight out of ten, you love it, we're ready to write. Do you have a suitcase with a million dollars in cash under your bed you'd pay with, or do you think we'd need to talk to a lender about financing?

Them

Definitely a lender. I've never done any of this before.

The line you do not cross

You did not ask what they earn, what they are approved for, or whether they are serious.

They told you anyway.

First time buying? Say congratulations and mean it. It is a genuinely exciting thing and almost nobody says it to them.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 18 / 31

slides.label: Five — is that date a guess, or a deadline?
slides.notes: Hardest of the five. The permission line goes first, every time. 'Six months feels right' and 'our lease is up in November' are different buyers and get different next steps.
slides.html:
Question five

Five — is that date a guess, or a deadline?

The hardest question of the five, and the one that decides everything you do next.

You

Have you thought about your timeline? Six months — relatively soon. Can I ask: is six months a default, like you figure it takes about that long? Or does something actually have to change for you to buy in six months?

Them

I mean — our lease is up in November.

First, get out of the way of yourself

I don't want you to feel like I'm interrogating you. I just want to make sure I'm scoping this all in the light of being to your benefit.

Never take the number

People give round timelines without thinking about them.

"Six months feels right" and "our lease is up" are different buyers.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 19 / 31

slides.label: Look at what you have, and what you never asked.
slides.notes: Sit on this one. Read the left column first, then the right. Five minutes, no screening questions, and they handed all of it over.
slides.html:
What you walk away with

Look at what you have, and what you never asked.

Five questions, about five minutes, standing on a sidewalk.

You never asked
What their budget is
Whether they are pre-approved
How serious they are
Whether they are working with anyone
Anything that sounds like screening
You walk away with
What they actually want, in their words
Whether they need financing
That this is their first purchase
A timeline — and the reason behind it
A house to compare everything against

That is the whole trick. Nobody hands this over to an interviewer. They hand it to someone who made it easy to talk.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 20 / 31

slides.label: Now the answer changes what you do.
slides.notes: Only the first branch gets a lender today. Say plainly that pushing a lender on a twelve-month buyer reads as pressure and costs you the relationship.
slides.html:
Three buyers

Now the answer changes what you do.

Three buyers walk out of that conversation. They do not get the same next step.

Writing now

No pre-approval?

Get them talking to a Zillow Home Loans officer. Today, not this week. This is the one branch with an immediate, concrete action.

Six months

Work it backwards.

Turn the date into a calendar with them, out loud. When do we tour, when do we talk to a lender, what is inventory doing right now.

Twelve months

Do not push a lender.

It makes no sense and it reads as pressure. Build the plan instead, and the cadence for staying in front of them without becoming noise.

All three are wins. The only loss is walking away with nothing.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 21 / 31

slides.label: Work the date backwards, out loud, with them.
slides.notes: Do this live with a volunteer if you have time. Use real closing timelines for your market — say the number out loud, do not round it.
slides.html:
The calendar

Work the date backwards, out loud, with them.

This is what turns "sometime next year" into something you can both put on a calendar.

1 How long to close? Whatever it actually runs in your market right now. Say the number.
2 So when do we need a lender? Count back from that. This is usually earlier than they think.
3 And what is inventory doing? If it is thin, touring starts sooner. Say why.
4 So we should be looking by — A month. Out loud. Written down. Agreed to.

You just earned a specific date to be back in front of them — instead of "checking in," which is what everybody else does and nobody wants.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 22 / 31

slides.label: Leave with an appointment. Not an intention.
slides.notes: This is the canonical version of the test — date, time, and the buyer knows what it is for. Everything later in the day refers back to this slide.
slides.html:
The test

Leave with an appointment. Not an intention.

A second appointment can be almost anything. It cannot be nothing.

Not an appointment
"I'll follow up"
"I'll send you some listings"
"Let me know if you see anything"
"We'll be in touch"
An appointment
A call with a lender, Thursday at six
A video call to map out the money
More homes, Saturday morning
A planning call, with their partner on it
The test is simple

Does it have a date, does it have a time, and does the buyer know what it is for? If all three are yes, you have momentum. If any one is missing, you have a feeling.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 23 / 31

slides.label: Now you say it.
slides.notes: Divider into the practice block. Two questions drilled in pairs, then the full closeout. Set the room up now: pairs, decide who is agent first.
slides.html:
Part four

Now you say it.

Two questions, one at a time, in pairs. You are not running the whole thing yet — you are getting the words out of your mouth until they sound like yours.

Why only two

Questions three and four are the easiest to run in context, so they get practiced inside the full roleplay instead.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 24 / 31

slides.label: Drill one — the open, and the rating.
slides.notes: Timebox tightly: three reps each, then back. Listen for anyone dropping the permission clause at the front of question one.
slides.html:
Drill 1 of 2

Drill one — the open, and the rating.

Questions one and two, back to back. Under thirty seconds of speech.

In your breakout room
Pairs. Decide who is the agent first.
Agent runs question one, then question two.
Buyer answers naturally — no acting, no difficulty.
Swap. Both of you go three times each.
Bring back

One sentence: what changed between your first attempt and your third?

Reminder

The first half of question one is what gives them permission to say no. Do not drop it.

You are practicing one question only. Do not run the rest of the closeout yet.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 25 / 31

slides.label: Drill two — the timeline, and the permission line.
slides.notes: The hard one. Tell buyers explicitly: only give up the real reason if the probe felt warm. That is the feedback the agent needs.
slides.html:
Drill 2 of 2

Drill two — the timeline, and the permission line.

Question five, with the line that goes in front of it. This is the hard one.

In your breakout room
Same pairs. Whoever went second last time is the agent first.
Buyer: give a round number — six months, next year.
Agent: use the permission line, then probe the number.
Buyer: only give the real reason if the probe was warm.
Bring back

The real reason behind the number — did the agent get it out of you, or not?

Reminder

If it came out as an interview, say so. That is the whole reason this one is drilled.

You are practicing one question only. Do not run the rest of the closeout yet.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 26 / 31

slides.label: Now the whole thing, start to finish.
slides.notes: Twelve to fifteen minutes total. Hand out buyer cards before they split. Remind them the buyer never shows the card — if the agent does not ask, they never learn it.
slides.html:
Full roleplay

Now the whole thing, start to finish.

You have just walked three houses with this person. Pick up at the sidewalk.

In your breakout room
Partner A is the agent first. Partner B plays the buyer.
Buyer: read your own card. Do not show it to anyone.
Agent: run all five questions, then land a next step.
Six minutes. Then swap and run it again.
Buyer gives feedback from the watch-for page.
Bring back

The next appointment you set — what it is for, the day, and the time.

The buyer never shows their card

Everything on it comes out only if the agent asks for it properly. If they never ask, you never say it.

Not a perfect closeout. A real one — with a real next step at the end of it.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 27 / 31

slides.label: Back together — what happened out there?
slides.notes: Two stories, not eight. Pick a pair that went differently from each other, and make the appointment get said out loud — purpose, day, time.
slides.html:
Debrief

Back together — what happened out there?

We are not looking for polish. We are looking for whether the questions did their job.

1 Who got a real reason? Whose buyer gave up the thing behind the timeline — and what opened it?
2 Who got interviewed? Buyers — did it ever start to feel like a form? When exactly?
3 What did you set? Say the appointment out loud. Purpose, day, time. All three or it does not count.
4 Who wanted to skip ahead? Anybody jump straight to the timeline? What did you lose by doing it?

Take two stories, not eight. Pick the pair that went differently from each other.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 28 / 31

slides.label: Before you drive away — three things.
slides.notes: Thirty seconds, in the car, before they drive off. Stage, note, task. Nothing moves the stage automatically yet — that is on them.
slides.html:
Follow Up Boss

Before you drive away — three things.

This is Day 1 again, thirty seconds of it, sitting in your car outside the house.

1 Move the stage Set it to Showing Homes. Nothing does this for you yet — it is manual.
2 Write the note What they liked, what they said would make it an eight, and their real timeline.
3 Set the task The appointment you just agreed to. Real date, real time, written as an action.

Do it in the car, not tonight. By tonight you will remember the houses and not the sentence that mattered.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 3 · 29 / 31

slides.label: Before Day 4 — one written exercise.
slides.notes: Read the three automatic fails out loud. The gap between 'six months' and 'lease is up in November' is the entire assignment.
slides.html:
Homework

Before Day 4 — one written exercise.

You will not have a live buyer yet, so this one runs on a scenario. It is graded.

What you submit
Their real criteria, in their words
Which of the three timelines this is — and your evidence
The date worked backwards, with real dates on it
The next appointment: purpose, day, time
Your Follow Up Boss note and task, as you would enter them
Fails regardless of score

Taking a stated timeline at face value when the buyer told you otherwise

Pushing a lender on a buyer whose timeline does not support it

Ending with no dated next step

The scenario has a buyer who says six months and then tells you their lease is up in November. That gap is the assignment.

slides.notes: Close on the five questions and the calendar. Then tee up Day 4: today they learned when to hand somebody to a lender; Day 4 is what happens when they do.
slides.html:
Zillow Preferred Onboarding • Day 3

The houses were the easy part.

Five questions, on a sidewalk, in your own words. Then a date on a calendar. That is the entire day.

Day 4

Financing, and Zillow Home Loans.

Today you learned when to hand somebody to a lender. Day 4 is what actually happens when you do.
